subject: biology
title: Limiting Factors & Light
welcome_lead: Today you'll work out what slows photosynthesis down — and use the inverse square law for light intensity.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Bioenergetics calculations — limiting factors, inverse square law, reading photosynthesis graphs.
final_note: You can now identify limiting factors from a graph, and apply the inverse square law to predict light intensity at different distances.

concepts.def: The factor that stops the rate going faster
Amount of light energy hitting an area
How much carbon dioxide is in the air
Flat part of a graph — rate stops rising
Best temperature for an enzyme (~25°C in plants)

walkthroughs.body_html:
Photosynthesis rate is controlled by whichever factor is in shortest supply. The three big ones are:

Light intensity — more light = more energy for the reaction.

CO₂ concentration — more CO₂ = more raw material.

Temperature — enzymes work best around 25°C. Too cold = slow. Too hot (~45°C+) = enzymes denature and rate crashes.

On a rate-vs-light-intensity graph, the line goes up at first, then plateaus (goes flat).

At the plateau, light is no longer limiting — adding more light won't help. Something else (CO₂ or temperature) is now the limiting factor.

To check: if you add extra CO₂ and the line jumps higher, then CO₂ was the limiting factor at the plateau.

Light spreads out from a lamp. Double the distance, and intensity drops to a quarter.

The rule: intensity ∝ 1 / d²

Example: a lamp 10 cm from pondweed gives intensity = 1/10² = 1/100 = 0.01 (in units of 1/cm²).

Move it to 20 cm: intensity = 1/20² = 1/400 = 0.0025.

That's one quarter of the original — because doubling distance squares the drop.

mcqs.q: On a rate vs light graph, what does the flat plateau tell you?
options: Light is now the limiting factor
Something other than light is now limiting
The CO₂ has run out completely
